**Small Theaters**

There is a particular hour, between ten and midnight, when the windows of apartment buildings become small theaters. Walking home, I catch fragments: a woman pacing with a phone pressed to her ear, her free hand carving the air; a man alone at a table set for two, the second chair empty; a child's silhouette pressed against glass, watching the street below as if it were a river.

Each window is a sentence torn from its paragraph. I invent the rest. The woman is ending an affair, or starting one, or telling her mother the test results were benign. The man has been stood up, or his wife works the night shift, or he simply prefers the geometry of an empty chair. The child is waiting for a parent who is late, or is not allowed outside after dark, or is rehearsing for a life that will never arrive.

What astonishes me is how much I believe these stories, how completely a stranger's life can be drafted in a glance and then abandoned at the next corner. We are all unreliable narrators of each other. And yet this is a kind of tenderness too — to be seen, even briefly, even wrongly, by someone who will never learn your name. The woman pacing will never know she became, for half a block, the heroine of a story about forgiveness. The city is full of unfinished sentences, and we carry them home like stones in our pockets, wondering whose life we borrowed.

There is a particular hour, between ten and midnight, when the windows of apartment buildings become small theaters. Walking home, I catch fragments: a woman pacing with a phone pressed to her ear, her free hand carving the air; a man alone at a table set for two, the second chair empty; a child's silhouette pressed against glass, watching the street below as if it were a river.

Each window is a sentence torn from its paragraph. I invent the rest. The woman is ending an affair, or starting one, or telling her mother the test results were benign. The man has been stood up, or his wife works the night shift, or he simply prefers the geometry of an empty chair. The child is waiting for a parent who is late, or is not allowed outside after dark, or is rehearsing for a life that will never arrive.

What astonishes me is how much I believe these stories, how completely a stranger's life can be drafted in a glance and then abandoned at the next corner. We are all unreliable narrators of each other. And yet this is a kind of tenderness too — to be seen, even briefly, even wrongly, by someone who will never learn your name. The woman pacing will never know she became, for half a block, the heroine of a story about forgiveness. The city is full of unfinished sentences, and we carry them home like stones in our pockets, wondering whose life we borrowed.
